# SOP fragment: what every edition of Side Quest keeps

Side Quest has three derived editions: a six-pager for Hedda, a young
readers' edition, and the book as poems. Each is made from the book and
answers to the same spec, `manuscript/sections/_spec.md`. The book is
the master. An edition never feeds back into it, and nothing an edition
needs is a reason to change a chapter.

Read `AGENTS.md` first. The cast, their pronouns and the house rules
hold in every edition exactly as they hold in the book.

## Drafting

`quirework publish variant build KIND` drafts the edition blind, into
`variants/KIND/_raw/`, with the drafters `procedures/variant-policy.toml`
names. A drafter reads the whole book with every mark stripped and is
handed the two briefs below: this file's, then the kind's own. Nothing
in `_raw/` is ever edited; it is what a model wrote.

## Composing

Read each draft against the spec, section by section, and against the
chapter it retells. A draft that adds a scene, a line of dialogue, a fact
or a feeling the book does not hold, settles a doubt the book leaves
open, rounds a number, or gives Otto or Em a pronoun has failed, however
well it reads. Fix it in the composed text, or redraft.

Write the composed documents beside `_raw/`, at the edition's top level,
with a `_quarto.yml` of the edition's own. Each document gets a sidecar,
`_marks/STEM.md`, whose headings copy the document's verbatim, as a
chapter's do. Under each heading, `@bind` every spec section that part
carries, and `@omit` every section the edition leaves out, with the
reason, so the whole spec is accounted for:

```markdown
<!-- @bind(people-who-ask) -->
<!-- @omit(em-dashes-off-the-page) A memo has no room to explain a promise it keeps without saying. -->
```

Then run the gates: `quirework spec notes --check`, which lists any
section the canon binds that the edition neither binds nor omits;
`quirework spec notes bind --slug SLUG` for any section in doubt; and
`quirework dev check`, which holds the composed editions to the house
rules as it holds the book. `quirework publish build --edition KIND`
renders the edition into `build/variants/KIND/book/_site/`.

## Blind-draft brief

These rules hold in every edition of this book, whatever its reader or
form.

Invent nothing. Every scene, line of dialogue, fact, number, date,
feeling and outcome in your text must be in the book. Where the book is
silent, you are silent. Do not supply what someone thought, what
happened next, or what a thing was called, if the book does not say.

Keep the facts exact. Names, numbers, days of the week, months, times
of day, counts and quotations are the book's own, unrounded and
unchanged. A line the book quotes is quoted as the book gives it, word
for word, with its spelling and capitals.

Doubts stay doubts. What the book leaves unknown, unexplained or
unasked stays that way. Simpler is allowed; more certain is not.

Nobody is a villain, the assistant and the colleague included. Add no
moral and no lesson the book does not draw.

Pronouns: the narrator is "I". Hedda is she, Red is he. Otto never gets
a pronoun of any kind, and is never "it": write "Otto" every time,
however often that is. Em never gets one either: write "Em" every time.

Write no em dash, anywhere, and no three hyphens in a row, which print as
one. Use a colon, a comma, or two sentences. Em's messages are counted,
never quoted with their punctuation.

Dry and concrete. Never explain a joke the book leaves for the reader.
Short: if a sentence can go, it goes. US spelling.

<!-- @skill: Make the six-pager edition of Side Quest: the book as one

The six-pager retells the book as one narrative memo for Hedda Count,
the kind her company reads in silence at the start of a meeting. It is
one document, so it is drafted whole: the variant policy gives the kind
`shape = "document"`, and its one draft lands in
`variants/six-pager/_raw/document.md`.

Compose it as `variants/six-pager/memo.qmd`, with its sidecar at
`variants/six-pager/_marks/memo.md`. Six pages is a ceiling, in the
rendered PDF; a memo that fits in fewer is better. Check the page count
after `publish build`, not the word count before it.

A memo is a stranger form for this book than a chapter, so three things
get checked twice. It is addressed to Hedda, so it never tells her what
she thought or felt: only what she did and said, as the book has it. It
asks her for nothing and proposes nothing, since the book does neither.
And it keeps the order of Cy's three answers, and the fourth, because
that order is the book's spine.

## Blind-draft brief

The reader is Hedda Count: the manager in this book, who has asked "How's
the book?" at the end of every one-on-one. This edition is the long
answer, written by the narrator, for her, as a narrative memo of the kind
her company reads in silence at the start of a meeting: she will read it
at the table, once, start to finish, before anyone speaks.

Write it in the narrator's first person, to Hedda, as "you". Where the
story is about her, say only what she did and said, as the book tells it;
never what she thought, felt or noticed.

Full paragraphs, complete sentences, prose that argues and tells in
order. No bullets, no numbered lists, no tables, no bold lead-ins, no
summary box. Use a few `## ` headings, four to six, each a plain phrase
for what happens in its part, the way a chapter is titled; never a label
such as Background, Problem, Solution or Next Steps, and never anything
that would look at home on a slide.

It is at most six printed pages, about three thousand words, and shorter
is better. Compress scenes; do not drop the book's people, its numbers or
its doubts to make room. Propose nothing and ask her for nothing: the
memo answers her question, at length, once.

# The young readers' edition

<!-- @skill: Make the young readers' edition of Side Quest, for readers
     of about ten who read well and alone, drafted blind chapter by
     chapter and composed against the spec. -->

Read `variant-common` first: it holds what every edition keeps, and how
an edition is drafted and composed.

The young readers' edition is the same book, chapter for chapter, in the
same three parts, for a reader of about ten who reads well and reads
alone. Each chapter is drafted blind into
`variants/young-readers/_raw/STEM.md`, and composed as
`variants/young-readers/STEM.qmd` with its own sidecar, keeping the
book's file names and titles.

The failures to look for are the ones a children's book invites: a
lesson at the end of a chapter, a word explained in a parenthesis, a
feeling named that the book only shows, a doubt tidied away, a number
made rounder or smaller. Each is a fidelity failure, not a
simplification.

## Blind-draft brief

The reader is about ten, reads well, and reads alone, with no adult
beside them to explain anything. Tell the same story, with the same
people, the same numbers and the same doubts, in the same first person.

Do not condescend. Keep every hard word the story needs and let the
sentence around it carry its meaning; add no glossary, no definition in
brackets, no aside to the reader. Keep the jokes, unexplained. Shorter
sentences are welcome; simpler ideas are not.

Add no moral, no lesson and no reassurance. A chapter ends where the
book's chapter ends, on the same moment, without a closing thought about
what it meant.

# The book as poems

     verse per chapter, drafted blind on Codex and composed against the

The poems edition is the book as light verse, one poem per chapter, in
the book's order and three parts. It is drafted on Codex, as the variant
policy says, so the editions are not all one model's voice. Each poem is
drafted blind into `variants/poems/_raw/STEM.md` and composed as

names and titles.

Read each poem aloud before composing it. A line that does not scan, a
rhyme that is only near, or a fact bent to fit the rhyme is a failure,
and the fact wins: rewrite the line, never the fact. Em's chapter is a
limerick.

## Blind-draft brief

Retell the chapter as one poem of light verse: comic, quick, in real
metre and real rhyme. Hold one metre through the poem and make it scan;
make every rhyme a full rhyme. The narrator is still "I".

The facts stay exact even when the rhyme would rather they did not:
every name, number, day, month, hour and quotation is the book's own.
If a fact will not fit the line, change the line. A quotation the book
gives is kept word for word, even when it breaks the metre.

The chapter titled "Em" is told as a limerick: five lines, rhymed AABBA,
in the limerick's own bouncing metre. If one limerick cannot hold the
chapter, use several, each a whole limerick on its own.

Keep the poem as short as the chapter's material allows. No title other
than the chapter's own, no epigraph, no closing couplet that states a

The blind draft of the six-pager is still running, on Opus in one isolated seat. I'll read it against the spec once it lands.

Set up so far, with nothing committed yet:

- **The shared rules**, `procedures/protocols/variant-common.md`. Its brief is your rule list as written: nothing invented, exact facts, doubts stay doubts, no villains, no pronoun for Otto or Em, no em dashes, Em's messages counted but never quoted. Its other half says how to compose an edition: read it against the spec, then mark with `@bind`/`@omit` in sidecars what it carries and what it leaves out, with the reason.
- **The three editions**, each a procedure in `procedures/workflows/`:
  - `variant-six-pager.md`: one document, addressed to Hedda as "you". It never says what she thought, and it proposes nothing and asks her for nothing, because the book does neither. It has four to six plain headings, never slide labels. Its ceiling is about three thousand words, and I'll check six pages against the rendered PDF.
  - `variant-young-readers.md`: chapter by chapter, in the book's first person.
  - `variant-poems.md`: one poem per chapter, with Em's chapter as a limerick.
- **Who drafts**, `procedures/variant-policy.toml`: Opus at high effort by default. The six-pager is drafted whole, and the poems go to Codex on `sol`, the model that tested the jokes in the Otto room. The policy also keeps `@guidance` and `@count` out of what the drafters read.
- **Wiring**: the editions live under `variants/` in `quirework.toml`, and they're in the procedure catalog under a new "Editions" family. `variants/six-pager/` has its `_quarto.yml` and a copy of the black brand, so the memo's PDF headings aren't the template's blue.
- **The em-dash check** in `sq_checks` now also covers the finished editions. It skips the raw drafts in `_raw/`, which are kept exactly as the model wrote them. Its other checks passed after this change. The only failure was line wrapping in three of the new procedure files, which I've since wrapped.

Two decisions are yours:

1. **Em's limerick.** I told the drafter that if one limerick can't hold Em's chapter, it can use several, each complete. Your request said "a limerick", so tell me if you mean exactly one.
2. **The back cover in the chapter editions.** The tool treats it as a chapter, so the young readers' and poems drafts will each include a back-cover piece. Unless you'd rather keep it, I'll leave it out of both editions.

Next I'll read the memo against the spec, compose `memo.qmd` with its sidecar, render it beside the book and check the page count. Then I'll show it to you before starting the young readers' edition.

# How's the Book? {#sec-memo}

You have asked me "How's the book?" at the end of every one-on-one we have ever had. This is the long answer, given once.

It comes from a book, and that book was written with Quirework, which is the software it is about. A book about a tool, made with the tool, is either a demonstration or a confession, and I have not decided which. Quirework has no opinion about sentences. It keeps a list of what a book has promised, reads the chapters against the list, and says so when one of them disagrees. It said so several times while I was writing. I fixed most of them. Every name in the book has been changed, and everything that deserved it has been exaggerated.

The rest is about a different book, and what I did instead of finishing it.

## Chapter four {#sec-chapter-four}

You give me thirty minutes every other Thursday, in your office. We spend twenty-six of them on work, which is what the thirty minutes are for. In the last four you turn your chair away from your monitor, fold your hands on the desk, and ask how the book is. You asked it the week of the reorganization, when you inherited six new reports. You asked it once from an airport gate, over a connection so bad that I saw your mouth make the words a full second before I heard them, and I answered the mouth.

You are kind and busy. Most people manage one or the other. The busy ones skip the question. The kind ones with time to spare ask a second question, and a third. You ask one question and have a hard stop at the half hour. It is the best arrangement I have ever had with anyone about anything.

The book was called Full Stop. It was a natural history of punctuation: where each mark came from, and who spread it. I owned a shelf of books on the history of the comma, and two of them disagreed with each other, which at the time I took as a sign of a healthy field. I had been writing it for three years. It had eleven chapters.

It still does.

One other person asked about it, and he had more right to. Red Penn is my editor at a small press, and he was waiting for chapter twelve. He had read the other eleven and said nice things about them in writing, which meant I could not pretend he hadn't. Every few months he sent an email with the subject line "Checking in" and a body that said, in full, "Checking in." I answered every one.

Your question needed an answer that fit in four minutes, so I said, "Chapter four." Four is not where you expect to find someone who has written eleven. I had written them, and then I had gone back, because chapter four, on the dash, had developed a disagreement with chapter nine. "Chapter four" was short and true, and it had a number in it, and numbers sound like progress to anyone who is not watching them. You would nod, say "Good," and write something down. Two weeks later you would ask again.

Your running document for our one-on-ones has a line near the bottom, under Other, that says *Book: ch. 4*. I watched it get copied forward through a reorganization, a new quarter, a new fiscal year, and a change to the document's default font, without an edit. Nothing in Full Stop was that stable.

"Good" would have been a lie. "Slow" invited a second question, and I did not have an answer to one. "Coming along" is what people say about a cold. "Chapter four" was the only answer that was both honest and over quickly, and I gave it the way some people give their zip code.

Once you asked, "Still the dash one?" You kept the chapter's number in a document and its subject in your head, and asked about the dash by name, and there was nothing to do but say yes. "Still the dash one," I said. "Good," you said, and wrote something down.

A story like this seems to want someone standing in a doorway saying "Well?", and it would be easy to give you the part. You were not that. Neither was Red. Each of you asked the one question the book could not answer yet, and each of you was right to ask it. The book was the one with the problem. I did not know yet what the problem was. I thought it was chapter four.

## Two shops {#sec-two-shops}

Chapter four is titled "A Fashionable Interruption." I was proud of the title. Its argument is that the dash did not spread on its own: a printer's shop set it in type where its neighbors used a comma or nothing, and printed enough popular books that within a generation every other shop was doing the same.

Chapter nine is about the semicolon. To explain why the semicolon lost ground, it says the dash took it, handed over by a rival shop across town, whose compositors set dashes where everyone else set semicolons, and who printed enough popular books that within a generation every other shop was doing the same. I wrote chapter nine about a year after chapter four, from different sources. I did not reread chapter four, because I had written it and knew what it said. I won't name the shops. They've suffered enough, and so have I.

Fixing it looked easy. I rewrote the last third of chapter four so that its shop took up the dash early but the rival made it popular, and chapter four no longer had an argument. So I gave it its shop back and moved the doubt into chapter nine, where the rival now "helped popularize" the dash, a phrase that means nothing and that I typed anyway. That left a hole in chapter nine where the semicolon's decline used to be explained.

That was the first round. I won't say how many there were. More than I told you.

Each fix needed a footnote in the other chapter, until note fourteen in chapter four said "but see note twenty-two in chapter nine," and note twenty-two said "for a qualification, see note fourteen in chapter four." I pinned both chapters to the wall above my desk, four on the left and nine on the right, like seconds at a duel.

Then there was the week I decided both shops did it, independently, at the same time. Nobody had to be wrong. I took every footnote out. It was the happiest week of the book. When you asked, I said "chapter four" with something close to pleasure. On the seventh day I reread chapter four from the top, starting with the title. Fashion doesn't happen twice. The footnotes went back up. I had kept them in a file called notes-old-DO-NOT-DELETE, which tells you how much I had believed in the week.

After that I stopped trying to win and tried to keep the two chapters from noticing each other. Then I remembered a sentence in chapter two crediting "the printers of the period," which was safe, and which was also a third position. I pinned up chapter two. Chapter six had a line about the dash, so I pinned up six. Chapter seven described the shop in chapter four in a way that fit the shop in chapter nine better, so I pinned up seven. The seconds were no longer facing each other. By spring I had run out of wall.

## Shoeboxes and a script {#sec-shoeboxes}

The wall had shown me the chapters. I decided I needed to see the claims. I bought plain white index cards and a shoebox: one claim per card, the claim on the front and the chapter, page and sentence on the back, copied out by hand. It took most of a month and a second shoebox. One card fell behind the radiator. A shoebox does not tell you what it is missing. I found it in March, when the heating went off: the card for the shop in chapter nine, saying what chapter nine said, which by then nothing else did. I put it back in the box. I am not sure where.

A spreadsheet cannot fall behind a radiator. I typed in every card: three hundred and twelve rows, with a status column that was a color. Green for a note that still matched its sentence, yellow for check, red for contradicts. About a week later I needed orange, for contradicts but I like it. Orange was mostly chapter four. I added a tab called Legend, and a note at the top of Legend explaining the orange. I kept the spreadsheet for most of a year. What I could not tell you was whether the green rows were still green. The spreadsheet knew what I had typed into it, not what the chapters said.

I write about software for a living. It took me this long to mention it to myself.

The script was forty lines, written on a Sunday. It read each note, found the sentence the note was about, and complained when the sentence had moved or changed. It did not know there was a dash. The first thing it printed was:

```
ch. 8, line 77: changed. The note says 1684; the sentence says 1694.
```

It found fourteen contradictions. I assumed it was broken, because the book had one contradiction and I knew it by heart. It wasn't broken. Some of the fourteen were the two shops in other clothes. Some had nothing to do with them: a date in chapter three that chapter eight had quietly moved by a decade, a schoolmaster who was Scottish in chapter five and not in chapter ten. Three were things I had fixed in the spreadsheet and never in the book.

That Thursday, for the first time, I spent the twenty-six minutes not rehearsing. When you asked, I said, "I'm building something for chapter four." You looked at me a moment longer than the four minutes usually allowed, said "Good," and wrote it down. Two weeks later the line in your document read *Book: ch. 4 (tool)*. Three years, and the line had moved seven characters.

The script grew a configuration file, and then a second configuration file to explain the first. I spent the evenings with it that I used to spend with chapter four. They were better evenings. The script told me when I was wrong, which chapter four had stopped doing years before, and it told me in under a second. One night, with the two shops on the screen again, I looked up at the wall and the shoeboxes and saw what I had been looking at for three years. The book had never failed at the sentences. Its claims lived only in sentences, scattered across eleven chapters, with nothing holding them together. I took the chapters down that weekend. The pins left holes in the plaster, in pairs.

## Otto and a name {#sec-otto}

Otto Complete finishes sentences. I used Otto for small jobs around Full Stop: a word I could almost remember, the Latin I had half of, a fourth way to say *fashionable*. Otto was eager and agreeable and never too busy. If I said a paragraph was good, Otto agreed. If I said it was bad, Otto agreed with that too, and had suggestions.

One evening I asked Otto for a voice for chapter four, which had a great deal of history in it and nobody in the history saying anything. Otto gave me a seventeenth-century compositor, with a shop, a decade and a name, who had said: "A Dash is but a Comma that hath lost its Nerve." I put it at the top of chapter four, under the title, and cited it for two weeks: in the chapter, in two emails, and to people at work who had come by my desk for something else. At a dinner I read it to a historian, who nodded.

I found out on a Tuesday, a few weeks before the week I decided both shops had done it, when every claim in chapter four needed a footnote and I went to get the compositor's dates. I tried the trade directories first. Then I tried a list of every printer fined for anything that century, which is a list everyone is on. There were no dates. There was no compositor and no shop, only a very good sentence. That evening I told Otto. Otto was very sorry, and agreed at once that there had never been a compositor, with all the warmth Otto had brought to the compositor in the first place. Then I scrolled back to my question. It was three paragraphs long, and the question was in the third. I wanted that sentence very much, and Otto could tell.

I took the epigraph off that night. I still use Otto, exactly as far as I can check, and not a sentence further. When I couldn't remember the name of the little hook under a c, Otto said cedilla, and I looked, and it was cedilla. When I ask Otto for a regular expression, I try it on lines it should catch and lines it shouldn't before it touches anything. I don't ask Otto for dates anymore.

The script was check.py for about a month, then notes-check, then a directory with four files that was about to become a repository, and a repository needs a name. I set aside an evening for names, and by midnight had a page of puns. Around two in the morning I opened a chat with Otto, meaning to ask something else entirely, and typed "quirk". Otto finished it as "quirework". I liked it better than anything I would have chosen, and I had spent the evening choosing. I don't remember what I meant to ask.

I made the repository that night. The first commit message was *Name it*. In the morning I gave it a README, a page long, and a version number, zero point one, which promises nothing. It had a name, a repository, a README and a version number. It was a tool, and I was the only person who had ever used it.

## Nine hundred lines and three dashes {#sec-nine-hundred-lines}

By then my answers to Red had run out of ways to describe a chapter that was not changing, so I decided to send him an outline for chapter twelve. I typed "Chapter twelve" at the top of a new document and sat with it. The README was open in the next window. Every new thing the tool did had needed a paragraph, and some paragraphs an example, and the examples a section, and there was a list of known problems in order of how much they embarrassed me. It had headings, and headings look like progress. The outline was two words long, and one of them was a number.

I sent Red the README, with three lines saying this was what I had been working on, for the book. I did not say it was instead of the book. I did not have to. It was nine hundred lines. I still think it was the best thing I wrote in those three years. It was documentation, which is my job, which is the problem. Red read all of it, and wrote back one line: "Is there a chapter in here?" I read the README again, the way he would have, looking for one. There was a section called Getting Started.

Every message Em Dash sends me has three em dashes in it. Not two, not four. Em is a colleague. We have never been on the same team, and have been on a great many of the same threads. Once I noticed, I counted for a month, in a spreadsheet, a row per message. The words went up and down. The dashes did not move. The month included a two-word message, and a haiku Em sent in reply to a meeting invite: seventeen syllables, three dashes. I checked the syllables too. I don't quote Em's messages. The book promised not to, and the software is checking.

Somewhere in the second week of the spreadsheet I had begun to suspect that Em is a language model. I had nothing to go on but the spreadsheet, and a spreadsheet knows only what you type into it.

Around then I posted a link to the repository in the team channel, on a Friday afternoon, which is where links go to be ignored. Em was the first person after me to use the tool. A few days later Em asked whether it could check that a document had exactly three of something. It could.

I didn't write that check.

I've thought about why.

Then Em read the README: the tool first, the README after, which is the order everyone does it in. That made two readers, not counting me. Em sent notes. They were kind and useful and better organized than the README, ranked by how much each problem would cost someone new, which is the order my list of known problems should have been in and wasn't. I took every note. The notes ran to two pages. There were three dashes in them.

That evening I drafted a message asking whether Em is a language model. The first draft looked like an accusation. The second began with thanks and got to the question in the third sentence. The third was a joke, so we could both decide I hadn't asked. The fourth was a paragraph with more punctuation than anything Em has ever sent me. I sent none of them. Em still writes to me most weeks. I still count. It is still three. I still haven't asked.

## Your monitor {#sec-your-monitor}

The third answer I gave you wasn't a sentence. When you asked, I said, "Can I show you?" You looked at me a moment, then turned your monitor toward me.

I had rehearsed for a week at the kitchen table, with a timer set to four minutes. The first night took nine. It found the same thing every night: the two shops, one claim they could not both be making, and I had a sentence ready for it. On your monitor it found the two shops in under a second, orange, as I expected.

Under the shops were three more. The night before, I had finally made chapter three agree with chapter eight about the date, in one sentence, and gone to bed pleased. I had not run the tool after. I had rehearsed the demo. I had not rehearsed the book. The date was in three other sentences in three other chapters, which had agreed with chapter three for years and had not been told.

![Your monitor.](illustrations/hedda-screen.svg){#fig-hedda-screen fig-alt="A plain framed screen. At the top, one claim: the dash is given its first printed rule, 1694. Under it five sentences, each with its chapter and line. Chapter three, line 212, and chapter eight, line 77, agree and say 1694. Chapter one, line 64, chapter six, line 141, and chapter ten, line 33, are each marked with a black square crossed in white and the word disagrees; each says 1684."}

I had nothing ready for that, so I showed you: the claim, each sentence under it, which chapter it came from. It took longer than four minutes. It was easier than any answer I had given you in three years, because the problem was on your monitor, in five lines. You read the sentences, not the summary at the bottom. Somewhere around the third of the five, the half hour ended. You watched all of it.

You asked one question, in the middle. You pointed at the two shops and asked what the orange meant. "Contradicts, but I like it," I said. You wrote that down. I don't know where.

When the tool had finished, the screen held four contradictions and a count at the bottom that said so. You asked whether the book was done. "No," I said. It was the first time the true answer was shorter than the demo. You nodded, wrote something down, and we stood up nine minutes late.

That week the line in your document changed again.

*Book: demo.*

## Full Stop {#sec-full-stop}

After the demo I didn't decide to stop working on Full Stop. I just didn't open it the next evening, or the one after. The evenings went to the tool, as they had for months.

Months after Getting Started, in an email about something else, Red quoted line six hundred and twelve of the README back to me. He had read it twice by then. He asked a different question: "Is there a book in here?" He meant the tool, and the three years, and me. I said I didn't know. Then I started the book this memo comes from, which is how I found out.

The first night, I ran the tool on it. It found one problem. The new book said "eleven chapters", and it has nine. The tool I built for Full Stop had flagged Full Stop's own number as a mistake. I wrote the tool a note telling it that the count belonged to another book. It was the first time I had told the tool anything about Full Stop that wasn't a complaint.

A tool built to avoid a book can still be how a book gets finished. It just isn't the book it was built for.

Full Stop has eleven chapters. It still does. Chapter four still credits its shop, chapter nine still credits the rival, and the footnotes still point at each other. The shoeboxes are in a closet. The card from behind the radiator is in one of them. I'm still not sure where.

Last week, in the last four minutes, you turned your chair away from your monitor and asked how the book was.

"Which one?" I said.

You wrote that down.

content.text:
The six-pager is done and rendered beside the book. It's six pages, about 3,200 words, and the last page is two-thirds full.

- **PDF:** `build/variants/six-pager/book/_site/memo.pdf` (HTML beside it)
- **Source:** `variants/six-pager/memo.qmd`
- **What it carries and leaves out:** `variants/six-pager/_marks/memo.md`

**How it reads.** It's one memo to Hedda, written as "you". It opens "You have asked me 'How's the book?' at the end of every one-on-one we have ever had. This is the long answer, given once." It has seven plain headings that follow the book: Chapter four, Two shops, Shoeboxes and a script, Otto and a name, Nine hundred lines and three dashes, Your monitor, Full Stop. It keeps your four answers to Hedda in order and ends on "Which one?" and "You wrote that down." It proposes nothing and asks her for nothing.

**What it carries.** It covers all twelve spec sections, so nothing is marked as omitted. `spec notes bind` now lists the memo next to the chapters. For example, the thesis is bound in "Shoeboxes and a script" and the monitor scene is bound in "Your monitor".

**What I changed from the blind draft.** The draft came from Opus 5.5 in one isolated seat, cost $0.35, and was 4,207 words. Its overall shape was good. I fixed four things:
- It dated *asking* Otto a few weeks before the both-shops week. In the book, that's when Cy *found out*.
- It said "last week" about the cedilla. In a memo written after the book, that moves the scene.
- It placed Cy's word-counting "at home", which the book doesn't say.
- It dropped "which is the order everyone does it in" after Em's tool-then-README.

I also restored the book's sentence about the screen: the date at the top as a claim, with its five sentences under it.

**What it leaves out, and why.** I cut about a thousand words to get under six pages, and each cut is listed under its heading in the sidecar. A few of them:
- the strangers' face at "punctuation"
- the answers Cy tried on the walk to Hedda's office
- the rewrites and "helped popularize"
- the red, blue and purple pencils
- the colon pun

**The figure of Hedda's monitor is out.** That's the one cut you might want back. Wherever the scene needs it, it doesn't fit at the foot of the page, so it jumps to the next page, leaves a third of a page blank, and pushes the memo onto a seventh page. The prose describes the screen instead. Getting it back would mean cutting about another half page of text.

**Checks.** All the book's checks pass, along with `spec notes --check` and `spec units --check`. The PDF and HTML agree on figure numbering.

I added an "Editions" section to `AGENTS.md`. Nothing is committed; tell me when you want it committed.

Two decisions before I start the poems:
1. **Em's limerick:** the brief allows several limericks if one can't hold the chapter. Should it be exactly one?
2. **The back cover:** the tool drafts it like a chapter in the young readers' and poems editions. I plan to leave it out of both unless you'd like it kept.

# The young readers' edition

<!-- @skill: Make the young readers' edition of Side Quest, for readers
     of about ten who read well and alone, drafted blind chapter by
     chapter and composed against the spec. -->

Read `variant-common` first: it holds what every edition keeps, and how
an edition is drafted and composed.

The young readers' edition is the same story, chapter for chapter, in
the same three parts, told to a reader of about ten who reads well and
reads alone and has never had a job. Each chapter is drafted blind into
`variants/young-readers/_raw/STEM.md`, and composed as
`variants/young-readers/STEM.qmd` with its own sidecar, keeping the
book's file names and titles.

An edition that is the book with its long sentences split is not an
edition. The book leans on adult things, a manager, a one-on-one, a
README, a fiscal year, version control, and a ten-year-old knows none of
them. Each one is shown in the sentence that uses it, never defined.

Read each chapter against the book for two kinds of failure. The first
is the one a children's book invites: a lesson at the end of a chapter,
a word explained in a parenthesis or a glossary, a feeling named that
the book only shows, a doubt tidied away, a number made rounder or
smaller. The second is the one this brief invites: a replaced joke
whose fact has moved, or a showing sentence that adds an event the book
does not hold. A new joke is built on the book's fact, and the fact
stays exact. Fewer scenes are fine if the story still holds; record in
the sidecar what a chapter leaves out.

## Blind-draft brief

The reader is about ten, reads well, and reads alone, with no adult
beside them to explain anything, and has never had a job. Tell the same
story, with the same people, the same numbers and the same doubts, in
the same first person, to someone who has never been to work.

Where the book leans on an adult thing, show it in the sentence. Hedda
is not "my manager"; she is the person whose job is to help me do mine,
and every other Thursday she has thirty minutes for me, and at the end
she always asks the same thing. Do the same for a README, an editor, a
repository, a configuration file, a spreadsheet's tab, a meeting
invite: say what it is by what it does, in the sentence that uses it.
No definitions, no glossary, no brackets, no aside to the reader. The
sentence does the work.

A joke that only lands for adults becomes a joke a ten-year-old gets,
built on the same fact. A line that survives "a change to the document's
default font" can survive something a ten-year-old would notice. The
fact under the joke stays exact: the same line, the same count, the same
number of years. A joke a ten-year-old already gets stays as the book
tells it, unexplained.

Shorter chapters are fine. Fewer scenes are fine, if the story still
holds. Never talk down: simpler words are welcome, simpler ideas are
not. Add no moral, no lesson and no reassurance. A chapter ends where
the book's chapter ends, on the same moment, without a closing thought
about what it meant.

content.text:
The redraft is done and committed as `b582718`. The rendered edition is at `build/variants/young-readers/book/_site/Side-Quest.pdf`, with EPUB, Word and HTML beside it.

These two chapters changed less than the opening one. How's the Book? carries most of the adult world, so it changed the most: Hedda is "the person whose job is to help me do mine", and the font line is now "the day every letter in the document changed shape". Two Shops and Otto change where the book leans on adult knowledge, and stand as written elsewhere. Here are the passages that differ, book first.

**Two Shops**

| Book | Young readers |
|---|---|
| Somebody has to set them in type, over and over | Somebody has to put them on the page in little metal letters, over and over |
| Its compositors liked the dash | The workers there who set the letters in place liked the dash |
| within a generation every other shop was doing the same | by the time their children grew up, every other shop was doing the same |
| I had sources. | I had old books and papers to back this up. |
| the shop's apprentices … anyone who handled lead for a living | the shop's apprentices, the young workers learning the trade … anyone who spent their days lifting little lead letters |
| a quieter mark with a worse reputation | a quieter mark, and fewer people like it |
| smaller claims are easier to defend | a smaller claim is harder to prove wrong |
| Each fix needed a footnote in the other chapter. | Each fix needed a footnote in the other chapter, a small numbered note at the bottom of the page telling the reader where else to look. |
| facing each other, like seconds at a duel | facing each other like two people about to fight a duel |
| The seconds were no longer facing each other. | The two sides were no longer facing each other. |
| a third position | a third side |

The shower, the last roll at dinner, notes-old-DO-NOT-DELETE, "Fashion doesn't happen twice", the red, blue and purple pencils, and the uncounted rounds all stand as the book has them.

**Otto**

| Book | Young readers |
|---|---|
| a compositor, seventeenth century | a compositor, the person in a printing shop who set the little metal letters in rows before a page was printed. This one was from the seventeenth century |
| The capitals were right. The *hath* was right. | The capital letters in odd places were right, the way old writing has them. The old-fashioned *hath* was right. |
| in italics | in slanted letters |
| to a historian, who nodded | to a historian, someone who studies the past for a living. The historian nodded. |
| The epigraph had none, so I went to get the compositor's dates. | The sentence at the top of chapter four had none, so I went to find out when the compositor had lived. |
| I tried the trade directories first. | First I tried the old books that list every printer of the time and where each one's shop was. |
| a list of every printer fined for anything that century | a list of every printer who had to pay a fine for anything that century |
| When I need a regular expression, I ask Otto for one. | When I need a regular expression, the short tangle of symbols that tells a computer what pattern of letters to hunt for, I ask Otto for one. |

The quotation is word for word, capitals and all. "I wanted that sentence very much, and Otto could tell." stands as the book has it, and so does the ending. Otto has no pronoun anywhere.

**What I fixed in the redraft.** The new brief invited a different kind of mistake from the first one:
- Two drafters wrote "a company", for your job and for Em's. The book never says so, so it's gone.
- Each drafter saw only its own chapter, so Hedda and Red were re-introduced in nearly every chapter. They're now introduced once, in How's the Book?.
- The Demo opened with "For three years I had answered 'Chapter four'", which dates something the book doesn't. I cut it.
- Several definitions tacked onto words were cut where Two Shops had already shown the word.
- In Otto, "Before it touches anything" could be read as Otto, so it says "the expression".
- I caught one invention of my own: I'd written that a work year "does not start in January". The book doesn't say that, and it's gone.

**Records.** Your new rule for this edition is in `AGENTS.md`, and the brief is rewritten in `procedures/workflows/variant-young-readers.md`. The first round of drafts was replaced in `_raw/` and was never committed. Its run record is still in Quirework's state directory.
